title: Information disclosure in HTTP headers
description: The web server reveals details about its software in HTTP response headers, such as the server type, software versions and framework. Headers that commonly leak this information include Server, X-Powered-By and X-AspNet-Version.
impact: An attacker can use these details to identify the technology stack and look up known vulnerabilities for the exact versions in use. This reduces the effort needed to plan a targeted attack.
recommendations: Remove or genericise headers that reveal software names and versions. For example, set server_tokens off in Nginx, set ServerTokens Prod and ServerSignature Off in Apache, and remove X-Powered-By and X-AspNet-Version in IIS or the application framework.
references: PortSwigger: Information Disclosure via HTTP Headers: https://portswigger.net/web-security/information-disclosure

title: Session token in URL
description: The application includes session tokens in its URLs. Browser history, server and proxy logs, and Referer headers sent to other sites can all record the token.
impact: An attacker who obtains a session token from any of these places can impersonate the user and access their data and functionality in the application.
recommendations: Do not put session tokens in URLs. Store them in cookies with the HttpOnly and Secure attributes. Expire session tokens after a period of inactivity and issue a new token at login.
references: CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/200.html

title: SSL certificate signed using a weak hashing algorithm
description: The service presents a certificate signed with a weak hashing algorithm, such as SHA-1, MD5, MD4 or MD2. These algorithms are vulnerable to collision attacks, which can let an attacker create a fraudulent certificate with the same signature.
impact: An attacker who forges a certificate with a valid signature can impersonate the service, intercept its traffic and lead clients to connect to the attacker instead of the legitimate service.
recommendations: Reissue the certificate with a signature that uses SHA-256 or a stronger hashing algorithm.
references: Microsoft Security Advisory: Feasibility of collision attacks against MD5: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security-updates/SecurityAdvisories/2008/961509
Shattered: Broken SHA-1 in Practice: https://shattered.io/

Microsoft: Configure SQL Server Database Engine for encrypting connections: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/database-engine/configure-windows/configure-sql-server-encryption?view=sql-server-ver16

title: Unsupported software
description: The system runs software that its vendor no longer supports, so it no longer receives security updates, patches or technical support. Vulnerabilities found after the end of support stay unpatched.
impact: Attackers target unsupported software because its vulnerabilities stay open. Exploiting them can give an attacker unauthorized access to the system and the data it holds.
recommendations: Upgrade to a supported version and apply all available security patches. Keep a software inventory with end-of-support dates so that upgrades can be planned before support ends.

title: Improper error handling
description: The application returns detailed error messages to users. These messages can include stack traces, database queries, file paths or configuration details that show how the application works internally.
impact: Error details help an attacker identify vulnerable components, database structures and authentication logic. This makes attacks such as SQL injection, remote code execution and privilege escalation easier to develop.
recommendations: Show users a generic error message and log the details on the server. Use custom error pages and a central error handler so that unhandled exceptions never reach the response. Disable debug mode in production.
references: CWE-209: Information Exposure Through an Error Message: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/209.html
PortSwigger: Information Disclosure via Error Messages: https://portswigger.net/web-security/information-disclosure

title: Default web server page
description: The web server shows its default page when a client requests the root URL. Default pages often reveal the server software and version, and suggest that the server has not been hardened.
impact: The page gives an attacker information for reconnaissance, such as the server software and version, which helps them choose targeted attacks.
recommendations: Remove or replace the default page, and remove any other default content and sample files that ship with the server.
references: Security issues of exposing default server home page: https://security.stackexchange.com/questions/194119/what-are-the-security-issues-of-exposing-default-server-home-page-in-public-inte

title: Deprecated TLS 1.0 and 1.1 supported
description: The service accepts connections over TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1. These protocol versions have known weaknesses, and RFC 8996 formally deprecated them in 2021.
impact: An attacker in a man-in-the-middle position may exploit these weaknesses to decrypt or modify traffic. Supporting these versions may also breach compliance requirements such as PCI DSS.
recommendations: Disable TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 and allow only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.

title: Vulnerable server software version
description: The server runs an outdated version of its software that has publicly known vulnerabilities.
impact: Depending on the vulnerabilities, an attacker may gain unauthorized access, execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service. A compromised server can also give an attacker access to other systems on the network.
recommendations: Update the server software to the latest stable release and apply security patches as the vendor releases them. Schedule regular patching so that components do not fall behind.
references: OWASP Top 10 A06:2021: Vulnerable and Outdated Components: https://owasp.org/Top10/A06_2021-Vulnerable_and_Outdated_Components/

title: Unauthenticated API access
description: One or more API endpoints respond without requiring authentication. Anyone who can reach the API can use these endpoints and the data and functions behind them.
impact: An attacker can read or change data, or perform actions, that should be limited to authenticated users. The impact depends on what the exposed endpoints do.
recommendations: Require authentication on every API endpoint that is not intended to be public, and check authorization on each request. Use a standard mechanism such as OAuth 2.0 access tokens.

title: Outdated libraries
description: The application uses outdated third-party libraries or dependencies that have known vulnerabilities.
impact: An attacker can exploit the published vulnerabilities in these libraries. Depending on the library, this can lead to attacks such as cross-site scripting or prototype pollution.
recommendations: Update the affected libraries to versions that fix the known vulnerabilities. Run a dependency scanner, such as npm audit or OWASP Dependency-Check, as part of the build to find vulnerable libraries.

title: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) header missing
description: The application does not set the Strict-Transport-Security header. This header tells browsers to connect to the site only over HTTPS.
impact: Without HSTS, a user's first visit, or a request to a typed http:// address, can go over plain HTTP. An attacker in a man-in-the-middle position can then use SSL stripping to downgrade the connection and intercept or modify traffic.
recommendations: Set the Strict-Transport-Security header on all HTTPS responses, for example Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains. Add the preload directive and submit the domain to the HSTS preload list once every subdomain supports HTTPS.
references: Google Chrome HSTS Preload List: https://hstspreload.org/

title: Clickjacking
description: The application can be loaded inside a frame on another site. An attacker can place the application in a hidden or disguised frame and trick users into clicking elements in it.
impact: A user who clicks on the attacker's page performs actions in the application without knowing it, such as changing account settings, approving a transaction or granting permissions.
recommendations: Set the Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive to 'none' or 'self'. For older browsers, also set the X-Frame-Options header to DENY or SAMEORIGIN.

title: Improper authentication mechanism
description: The application does not verify user identity reliably. Common causes are weak password policies, missing multi-factor authentication (MFA), hardcoded credentials and authentication checks that can be bypassed.
impact: An attacker can gain access to accounts through brute force, credential stuffing or by bypassing the check, and then act as the legitimate user.
recommendations: Enforce MFA, a strong password policy and rate limiting on login attempts. Check authentication on the server for every protected request. Use a standard protocol such as OpenID Connect instead of a custom scheme.

title: Improper session termination
description: The application does not invalidate sessions on logout or after inactivity, so session tokens stay valid after the user has left.
impact: An attacker who obtains a session token can keep using it after the user logs out, to access data or perform actions as that user.
recommendations: Invalidate the session on the server when the user logs out, and expire sessions after a period of inactivity. Revoke any associated tokens at the same time. Set the HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite attributes on session cookies.

title: Weak password policy
description: The application lets users choose short or common passwords. Common weaknesses are a low minimum length, no check against lists of breached passwords and no multi-factor authentication (MFA).
impact: Attackers can guess weak passwords with brute-force, dictionary or credential stuffing attacks and take over accounts.
recommendations: Require at least 12 characters and reject passwords that appear in breached-password lists. Offer or enforce MFA. NIST SP 800-63B recommends length requirements and breached-password checks over complexity rules and forced periodic changes.
references: NIST SP 800-63B: Digital Identity Guidelines, Authentication: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html

title: User enumeration
description: The application reveals whether a username or email address exists through differences in its responses. The differences can be in error messages, response times or HTTP status codes on the login, registration or password reset pages.
impact: An attacker can build a list of valid accounts and then target them with password guessing, credential stuffing or phishing.
recommendations: Return the same message, status code and response time whether or not the account exists, for example "Invalid username or password". Apply rate limiting to login, registration and password reset requests.
references: OWASP Top 10: Identification and Authentication Failures: https://owasp.org/Top10/A07_2021-Identification_and_Authentication_Failures/

title: Insecure direct object reference (IDOR)
description: The application gives access to objects, such as database records, files or accounts, based on an identifier that the user supplies, without checking that the user may access that object. An attacker can change the identifier in a URL, API request or form to reach other users' data.
impact: An attacker can read, change or delete data that belongs to other users. Depending on the objects exposed, this can lead to account takeover or tampering with transactions.
recommendations: Check on the server that the current user is authorized to access each requested object. Random identifiers such as UUIDs make enumeration harder, but they do not replace the authorization check.
references: OWASP: Insecure Direct Object Reference Prevention Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Insecure_Direct_Object_Reference_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/639.html

title: Unrestricted file upload
description: The application does not restrict the type, content or size of uploaded files, and stores them where they can be reached or executed. An attacker can upload scripts, executables or other harmful content.
impact: If the server executes an uploaded file, such as a web shell, the attacker gains remote code execution and can take over the server. Attackers can also use uploads to host malware or phishing pages, or to fill the disk.
recommendations: Allow only the file types the feature needs, and check the file content, not only the extension and Content-Type header. Store uploads outside the web root, give them random names and block execution in the upload directory. Limit file size and require authentication to upload.
references: CWE-434: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/434.html

title: Local file inclusion (LFI) and path traversal
description: The application builds a file path from user input without restricting it to the intended files. An attacker can use sequences such as ../../etc/passwd to read files outside the intended directory, or make the application include and run a local file.
impact: An attacker can read configuration files, credentials and source code. If the application includes the file as code and the attacker can place content on the server, for example through a file upload or a log file, this can lead to remote code execution.
recommendations: Do not build file paths from user input. If the user must choose a file, map the choice to an allowlist of known files. Never pass user input to include() or require() in PHP. Run the application with file permissions limited to the files it needs.
references: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ("Path Traversal"): https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/22.html

title: HTTP Basic authentication
description: The application uses HTTP Basic authentication, which sends the username and password with every request, encoded in Base64. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption, and Basic authentication has no logout or session expiry.
impact: If the credentials travel over plain HTTP, an attacker who can observe the traffic can decode and reuse them. Browsers also keep the credentials until they close.
recommendations: Replace Basic authentication with a session-based or token-based mechanism. If Basic authentication must stay, serve it only over HTTPS and limit it to low-risk or internal resources.
references: CWE-1391: Use of Weak Authentication Scheme: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1391.html

title: Missing antivirus protection
description: The system has no antivirus or anti-malware protection.
impact: Malware such as ransomware, spyware or trojans can run on the system undetected. An attacker can use it to steal credentials, keep persistent access or spread to other systems.
recommendations: Install endpoint protection with real-time scanning and automatic signature updates, and monitor its alerts centrally.
references: NIST SP 800-83 Rev. 1: Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/83/r1/final

title: Privilege escalation
description: A user can gain privileges beyond those they were granted. Vertical escalation gives a user higher privileges, such as administrator or root. Horizontal escalation gives a user access to another account at the same privilege level. Common causes are misconfigurations, unpatched vulnerabilities and weak access controls.
impact: An attacker with elevated privileges can run arbitrary commands, read or change sensitive data, change system settings and disable security controls. Privilege escalation is often a step towards persistent access, lateral movement and ransomware deployment.
recommendations: Grant users and services only the permissions they need. Patch the operating system, applications and third-party components regularly. Check authorization on the server for every privileged action, and monitor for unexpected privilege changes.
references: PortSwigger: Access control vulnerabilities and privilege escalation: https://portswigger.net/web-security/access-control

title: Unencrypted communications
description: The service sends data over the network without encryption, for example over HTTP, FTP, Telnet, or SMTP without TLS.
impact: An attacker who can observe the traffic can read credentials, session tokens and other sensitive data, and can modify the traffic in transit.
recommendations: Replace unencrypted protocols with encrypted ones, such as HTTPS, SFTP, SSH and SMTP with TLS, and use TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3. For web applications, redirect HTTP to HTTPS and set the Strict-Transport-Security header.
references: OWASP: Transport Layer Security Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Transport_Layer_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html
CWE-319: Cleartext Transmission of Sensitive Information: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/319.html

title: Weak cipher suites supported
description: The service accepts cipher suites that use weak algorithms, such as RC4, DES, 3DES or export-grade ciphers, or that use MD5 for integrity. These algorithms are vulnerable to known attacks, such as Sweet32 against 3DES.
impact: An attacker in a man-in-the-middle position may be able to decrypt or modify traffic that uses one of these cipher suites.
recommendations: Disable weak cipher suites and allow only suites that use AEAD ciphers, such as AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305, over TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.
references: OWASP: Transport Layer Security Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Transport_Layer_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html
CWE-327: Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/327.html

title: SSH Terrapin prefix truncation (CVE-2023-48795)
description: The SSH server supports the chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com cipher, or CBC-mode ciphers combined with Encrypt-then-MAC (-etm@openssh.com) MAC algorithms, without strict key exchange. The Terrapin attack (CVE-2023-48795) uses these modes to remove messages from the start of the encrypted channel without either side noticing.
impact: An attacker in a man-in-the-middle position can downgrade security features of the connection, for example by disabling keystroke timing obfuscation or extensions negotiated during the handshake. In some SSH implementations this can lead to further attacks.
recommendations: Update the SSH server and clients to versions that support strict key exchange, such as OpenSSH 9.6 or later. Until then, disable chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com and the -etm@openssh.com MAC algorithms when used with CBC ciphers, and use AES-GCM or AES-CTR instead.
references: CVE-2023-48795: SSH Terrapin Prefix Truncation Weakness: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2023-48795

title: Weak SSH ciphers supported
description: The SSH server accepts weak algorithms, such as the 3des-cbc, arcfour or blowfish-cbc ciphers, or MAC algorithms based on MD5 or truncated 96-bit hashes.
impact: An attacker in a man-in-the-middle position may be able to decrypt or modify parts of the SSH session. Supporting these algorithms may also breach compliance requirements.
recommendations: Remove weak ciphers and MAC algorithms from the SSH server configuration. Allow only ciphers such as aes256-gcm@openssh.com, aes128-gcm@openssh.com and aes256-ctr, and MAC algorithms such as hmac-sha2-256 and hmac-sha2-512.

title: Cross-site scripting (XSS), reflected
description: The application includes user input from a request in its response without encoding it. An attacker can craft a link that carries a JavaScript payload, which runs in the victim's browser when they open the link.
impact: The script runs with the victim's access to the application. An attacker can steal session cookies, perform actions as the victim, change page content or redirect the victim to a malicious site. The victim has to open the link, so attackers send it through phishing emails or messages.
recommendations: Encode user input for the context where it appears in the page, such as the HTML body, an attribute or JavaScript. Validate input against the expected format. Set a Content Security Policy to restrict which scripts can run, and set the HttpOnly flag on session cookies.
references: OWASP: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Prevention Cheat Sheet: https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/xss/
CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('XSS'): https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/79.html

title: Cross-site scripting (XSS), stored
description: The application stores user input, such as comments, messages or profile fields, and later displays it to other users without encoding it. Unlike reflected XSS, the payload runs for every user who views the affected page, without the attacker sending them a link.
impact: The attacker's script runs in the browser of every user who views the content. It can steal sessions, perform actions as those users, capture keystrokes or spread malware. If an administrator views the content, the attacker may gain administrative access.
recommendations: Encode stored data for the context where it is displayed, and validate input before storing it. Set a Content Security Policy to restrict which scripts can run, and set the HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite flags on session cookies.
references: OWASP: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Prevention Cheat Sheet: https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/xss/
CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('XSS'): https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/79.html

title: Cross-site scripting (XSS), DOM-based
description: The application's client-side JavaScript writes user-controlled data into the page through unsafe functions, such as innerHTML, document.write() or eval(), or into location.href. The browser handles the payload entirely, so the server may never see it.
impact: As with other XSS, the attacker's script runs in the victim's browser and can steal sessions or perform actions as the victim. Server-side filtering and web application firewalls may miss the attack, because the payload can stay in the URL fragment and never reach the server.
recommendations: Use safe DOM APIs such as textContent instead of innerHTML, and do not pass user data to eval() or similar functions. If the application must render HTML from user input, sanitize it with a library such as DOMPurify. Set a Content Security Policy, and consider Trusted Types to block unsafe DOM writes.
references: OWASP: DOM XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet: https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/DOM_Based_XSS
CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('XSS'): https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/79.html

title: SQL injection
description: The application builds SQL queries from user input without separating code from data. An attacker can change the structure of the query and run their own SQL commands. Login forms, search fields and API parameters are common places for this flaw.
impact: An attacker can bypass authentication and read, change or delete data in the database, including credentials and personal data. On some database configurations, the attacker can also run operating system commands.
recommendations: Use parameterized queries or prepared statements for every query, or an ORM that parameterizes queries, such as SQLAlchemy or Hibernate. Validate input against the expected format. Connect to the database with an account that has only the permissions the application needs.
references: OWASP: SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet: https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/SQL_Injection
CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in SQL Commands ('SQL Injection'): https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/89.html

title: NoSQL injection
description: The application builds NoSQL queries from user input without validating it. An attacker can submit query operators, such as MongoDB's $ne or $gt, in place of plain values and change what the query does. Databases such as MongoDB, CouchDB and Elasticsearch can be affected.
impact: An attacker can bypass authentication, read or change data and, in some cases, run server-side JavaScript. If the database stores sessions or tokens, the attacker can take over accounts.
recommendations: Check that each input has the expected type, for example a string rather than an object, and reject keys that start with $. Use the driver's query builders or an ODM with strict schemas, such as Mongoose. Give the database account only the permissions the application needs.
references: OWASP WSTG: Testing for NoSQL Injection: https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/07-Input_Validation_Testing/05.6-Testing_for_NoSQL_Injection
CWE-943: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in NoSQL Queries: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/943.html

title: Server-side template injection (SSTI)
description: The application inserts user input into a server-side template, so the template engine evaluates it as template code. Engines such as Jinja2, Twig, FreeMarker, Velocity and Pug can be affected.
impact: Depending on the engine, an attacker can read sensitive data, such as environment variables that hold database credentials or API keys, or execute arbitrary code and take over the server.
recommendations: Pass user input to templates as data, never as part of the template source. If users must be able to edit templates, use a sandboxed environment, such as Jinja2's SandboxedEnvironment or Twig's sandbox extension, and restrict the functions available to it.
references: OWASP WSTG: Testing for Server-side Template Injection: https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/07-Input_Validation_Testing/18-Testing_for_Server-side_Template_Injection
CWE-1336: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Template Engines: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1336.html

title: Server-side request forgery (SSRF)
description: The application makes requests to a URL that the user supplies, without restricting where the request can go. An attacker can make the server send requests to internal systems or to other external hosts.
impact: An attacker can reach services that are not exposed to the internet, such as internal APIs, admin interfaces or cloud metadata services like the AWS instance metadata endpoint at 169.254.169.254. Metadata services can expose cloud credentials, which may lead to wider compromise.
recommendations: Allow requests only to the hosts the feature needs. Resolve the hostname, block private, loopback and link-local addresses, and check again after each redirect. On AWS, require IMDSv2. Restrict the server's outbound network access with firewall rules.

title: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)
description: The application accepts state-changing requests without checking that they came from its own pages. An attacker can make a logged-in user's browser send a request to the application, for example from a malicious site, and the browser attaches the user's cookies.
impact: An attacker can perform actions as the victim, such as changing their email address or password, transferring funds or, for an administrator, changing application settings.
recommendations: Require an anti-CSRF token in every state-changing request and check it on the server. Set the SameSite attribute on session cookies to Lax or Strict. Check the Origin header on sensitive requests, and ask users to re-authenticate before critical actions.

title: Command injection
description: The application passes user input to an operating system shell, for example through exec(), system() or popen(), without validating it. An attacker can add their own commands to the input.
impact: An attacker can run arbitrary commands on the server with the application's privileges. This usually leads to full compromise of the server and access to its data and credentials.
recommendations: Avoid calling the shell. Use a library function for the task, or run the program directly with its arguments passed as a list, for example subprocess.run() in Python with shell=False. Validate input against an allowlist of expected values. Run the application with the least privileges it needs.
references: CWE-78: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in OS Command: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/78.html

title: XML injection and XML external entities (XXE)
description: The application parses XML that contains user input, and the parser allows document type definitions (DTDs) and external entities. An attacker can change the structure of the XML or define external entities that the parser resolves.
impact: With XXE, an attacker can read files from the server, make the server send requests to internal systems (SSRF) or cause a denial of service. Changing the XML structure can also alter application logic or bypass access controls.
recommendations: Disable DTDs and external entity processing in the XML parser. Validate input before adding it to XML documents, and build XML with a library rather than string concatenation. Use a simpler format such as JSON where the application does not need XML.
references: OWASP: XML External Entity Prevention Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/XML_External_Entity_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
CWE-91: XML Injection (aka Blind XPath Injection): https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/91.html
PortSwigger: XML external entity (XXE) injection: https://portswigger.net/web-security/xxe

title: LDAP injection
description: The application builds LDAP queries from user input without escaping special characters, so an attacker can change the query filter. Applications that use Active Directory, OpenLDAP or other directory services for login or lookups can be affected.
impact: An attacker can bypass authentication, read directory data such as user and group details and, in some cases, change directory entries.
recommendations: Escape user input with the LDAP library's escaping functions before adding it to a filter or distinguished name. Validate input against an allowlist that rejects characters such as *, (, ), & and |. Bind to the directory with an account that has only the permissions the application needs, and use LDAPS.
references: CWE-90: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in LDAP Queries: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/90.html
OWASP: LDAP Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/LDAP_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html

title: Server-side includes (SSI) injection
description: The web server processes server-side include directives in pages that contain user input. An attacker can submit directives, such as <!--#exec cmd="id" -->, that the server executes. Servers that parse .shtml, .shtm or .stm files can be affected.
impact: An attacker can read files on the server and, if the exec directive is enabled, run operating system commands. This can lead to full compromise of the server.
recommendations: Disable SSI processing if the site does not use it. If it does, disable the exec directive and encode user input so that it cannot form SSI directives.
references: CWE-97: Improper Neutralization of Server-Side Includes (SSI) Within a Web Page: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/97.html
OWASP WSTG: Testing for SSI Injection: https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/07-Input_Validation_Testing/08-Testing_for_SSI_Injection

title: Remote file inclusion (RFI)
description: The application includes a file whose location comes from user input, and the input can be a remote URL. An attacker can make the application load and run code from a server they control. PHP applications that pass user input to include() or require() are the most common case.
impact: The attacker's code runs on the server with the application's privileges, which gives them remote code execution. Attackers use RFI to install web shells and persistent backdoors.
recommendations: Set allow_url_include=Off in the PHP configuration. Do not build include paths from user input. If the user must choose a file, map the choice to an allowlist of known files.
references: OWASP WSTG: Testing for File Inclusion: https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/07-Input_Validation_Testing/11.1-Testing_for_File_Inclusion
CWE-98: Improper Control of Filename for Include/Require Statement: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/98.html

title: HTTP request smuggling
description: The front-end server, such as a load balancer, reverse proxy or CDN, and the back-end server disagree on where one HTTP request ends and the next begins. The usual cause is different handling of the Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding headers. An attacker can hide a second request inside the first.
impact: An attacker can bypass front-end security controls, capture other users' requests along with their session cookies, and poison caches.
recommendations: Use HTTP/2 end to end where possible. Configure the front-end server to normalize ambiguous requests and to reject requests that contain both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding headers. Keep the front-end and back-end server software up to date.
references: OWASP WSTG: Testing for HTTP Splitting and Smuggling: https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/07-Input_Validation_Testing/15-Testing_for_HTTP_Splitting_Smuggling
CWE-444: Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/444.html

title: Host header injection
description: The application trusts the Host header of the request, for example to build absolute URLs or route requests. An attacker can send a request with a Host header they control.
impact: An attacker can poison password reset emails with links to their own domain and capture the reset tokens. Depending on the setup, this can also lead to web cache poisoning or to SSRF against internal virtual hosts.
recommendations: Configure the web server to reject requests with unrecognized Host values. Build absolute URLs from a configured domain name, not from the Host header. If the application sits behind a reverse proxy, trust X-Forwarded-Host only when the proxy sets it.
references: OWASP WSTG: Testing for Host Header Injection: https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/07-Input_Validation_Testing/17-Testing_for_Host_Header_Injection
CWE-640: Weak Password Recovery Mechanism for Forgotten Password: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/640.html

title: Open redirect
description: The application redirects users to a URL taken from user input, such as a query parameter, without validating it. An attacker can create a link on the legitimate domain that sends users to a malicious site.
impact: Users trust the link because it starts with the legitimate domain, so attackers use it in phishing to send users to fake login pages. Open redirects can also help other attacks, such as stealing OAuth tokens through a crafted redirect_uri.
recommendations: Do not redirect to URLs taken from user input. If the target must come from the user, map it to an allowlist of destinations, or accept only relative paths on the same site.
references: OWASP: Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Unvalidated_Redirects_and_Forwards_Cheat_Sheet.html
CWE-601: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site ('Open Redirect'): https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/601.html

title: Misconfigured cross-origin resource sharing (CORS)
description: The application's CORS policy lets untrusted origins read its responses. Common causes are reflecting any Origin header back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin, trusting the null origin, or matching origins with a loose pattern, combined with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.
impact: A malicious site can send requests to the application from a logged-in user's browser and read the responses. This exposes the user's data, API responses and any tokens returned in them.
recommendations: Allow only a fixed list of trusted origins in Access-Control-Allow-Origin, and send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true only for those origins. Never reflect the Origin header without checking it, and do not trust the null origin.
references: OWASP WSTG: Testing Cross Origin Resource Sharing: https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/11-Client-side_Testing/07-Testing_Cross_Origin_Resource_Sharing

title: Account lockout
description: The application's account lockout policy is missing or too strict. Without lockout or rate limiting, attackers can guess passwords without limit. With a strict or permanent lockout, attackers can lock users out on purpose.
impact: If lockout is missing or too lenient, attackers can brute-force passwords or use credential stuffing to take over accounts. If lockout is too strict, an attacker can lock out many accounts at once and deny users access, which also raises support costs.
recommendations: Increase the delay between login attempts after each failure instead of locking accounts permanently. Enforce MFA. Provide account recovery that verifies the user's identity, and monitor failed logins for signs of an automated attack.
references: CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts: https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/307.html

title: Web cache poisoning
description: A cache, such as a CDN or reverse proxy, stores a response that an attacker has influenced and serves it to other users. This happens when the response depends on an input, such as a header, that is not part of the cache key.
impact: Every user who receives the poisoned response gets the attacker's content, such as injected JavaScript, a redirect or a fake login form. The attack affects all visitors to the page until the cache entry expires.
recommendations: Include every input that changes the response in the cache key, using the Vary header where needed, or stop the application from using that input. Do not cache responses that contain user-specific data. Disable headers the application does not need, such as X-Forwarded-Host.
